passage: During recess at the school playground, Gurleen picked up a flat leaf and a twig. "This is my plate, and this is my spoon." Kiran grabbed a bigger stick. "This is my microphone! Welcome to the cooking show!" Gurleen served pebbles as "parathas" on her leaf. Kiran pretended to taste. "Too spicy!" he gasped, fanning his mouth. When the bell rang, Gurleen carefully tucked her leaf-plate under a bench for tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Kiran use as a microphone?
qa.a: He used a bigger stick as a microphone.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen tuck her leaf-plate under the bench?
qa.a: She was fond of her leaf-plate and wanted to keep it for tomorrow, since it still mattered to her as a real plate in their game.

qa.q: How could a teacher encourage this kind of play?
qa.a: Leave some natural bits like leaves and sticks around and ask the children about their pretend show.

qa.q: How might Kiran see Gurleen's pebble parathas?
qa.a: He treats them as real food, playing along and making the story funnier for both of them.

grounding: Two children use leaves, twigs and pebbles to stand for plates, spoons, food and a microphone.

passage: My brother Irfan is four. Yesterday he held Abbu's slipper to his ear and talked into it. "Hello, Nani? Yes, I ate lunch." I laughed and picked up the slipper to put it back. He shouted, "You cut my call!" and stomped off. Later he used a folded chapati as a boat in his plate and his spoon as a sail. I said sorry about the phone. — Harsha

qa.q: What did Irfan use as a phone?
qa.a: He held Abbu's slipper to his ear and talked into it.

qa.q: Why did Irfan shout and stomp off?
qa.a: He felt angry and resentful that Harsha had ended his pretend call; to him the slipper really was a phone.

qa.q: What could Harsha do next time to respect Irfan's pretend play?
qa.a: Harsha could ask first, like "Can I have the phone after your call?", before moving his toy.

qa.q: How might Harsha see the slipper differently from Irfan?
qa.a: To Harsha it was just a slipper out of place, while to Irfan it was an important phone connected to Nani.

grounding: An older sibling describes a little brother using a slipper as a phone and a chapati as a boat, and his anger when the pretence is broken.

passage:
Monday: Vinita pushed a steel spoon along the table. "Vroom, car!" Her father Darshan asked, "Where is it going?" "School," she said.
Friday: She dragged an empty carton into the hall. "This is a boat. Papa, you're the fish." She paddled with a ruler.
The next Sunday: A towel became her cape, a hairbrush her phone and a cushion a sleeping horse. "Shh, Papa, Horsey is sleeping." Darshan tiptoed past.

qa.q: What did Vinita use as a car on Monday?
qa.a: She used a steel spoon as a car.

qa.q: What does Vinita's "Shh, Papa, Horsey is sleeping" show about her thinking?
qa.a: It shows she treats the cushion as a real horse she cares for and wants Papa to respect her pretend world.

qa.q: How did Darshan support her pretend play?
qa.a: He asked where the car was going and tiptoed past the sleeping horse, joining in without taking over.

qa.q: What is it like for Darshan to be part of this game?
qa.a: He gets pulled into her stories as a fish and a quiet passer-by, which lets him share her imagination. 😊

grounding: Over days, a girl uses more objects to stand for others in pretend play.

passage: The movers had packed every toy by noon, and rain kept Anirban indoors. He wandered, bored. Then he grabbed Seema's ladle. 'Hello, hello, mic testing!' He sang into it. A bedsheet over two chairs became his stage. A folded newspaper became a ticket. 'Didi, you're the audience.' Seema, wrapping plates, sighed, 'Two minutes only.' She clapped when he bowed, then took her ladle back.

qa.q: What did Anirban use as a microphone?
qa.a: He used Seema's ladle as a microphone.

qa.q: How was Seema feeling when she said 'Two minutes only'?
qa.a: She seemed tired and busy with packing, a bit impatient, but willing to join his game briefly.

qa.q: How could Seema keep Anirban busy while she packs?
qa.a: She could hand him a few safe objects, like an empty box or a cloth, and let his pretend show go on nearby.

qa.q: What would change if Anirban's toys had not been packed?
qa.a: He might have played with his usual toys and not needed to turn a ladle and bedsheet into a stage.

grounding: Illustrates a child using everyday objects to stand for other things in pretend play despite a constraint.

passage: In their Mumbai flat, Omkar picked up Aai's rubber chappal and held it to his ear. 'Hello? Pizza uncle?' Reena, his older sister, grinned and grabbed a remote. 'Hello, this is Pizza Shop.' Omkar ordered 'ten pizzas and one ice cream', then galloped off on the sofa cushion, his horse. 'Delivery!' He handed Reena a flat book: the pizza. She pretended to take a huge bite.

qa.q: What did Omkar use as a phone?
qa.a: He used Aai's rubber chappal.

qa.q: What does Omkar galloping off with 'Delivery!' suggest about his mood?
qa.a: It suggests he was excited and fully caught up in the story, enjoying making things stand for other things.

qa.q: How could Reena help his pretend play grow?
qa.a: She can keep playing along and add small twists, like saying the pizza is too hot, so he invents new responses.

qa.q: What is it like for Reena to join her brother's game?
qa.a: It seems fun for her too, since she jumps in with a remote and pretends to take a big bite. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young child using objects as symbols for other things in pretend play in an urban home.

passage:
"Hello? Hello, Papa?" Chandrika held a banana to her ear.
Vijay looked up from his newspaper. "Who's calling?"
"It's the doctor. For you." She held out the banana.
He took it. "Hello, doctor. Yes... yes... my daughter needs a bath? Okay."
"No! Doctor said ice cream!"
"Ah, sorry, bad line." He gave it back.
Chandrika, five, pressed buttons on the banana. "Now I'm calling Nani." Then she peeled it and ate the phone.

qa.q: What did Chandrika use as a phone?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's shout "Doctor said ice cream!" suggest?
qa.a: She was enjoying the game and felt cheeky, wanting to steer the pretend call her way.

qa.q: What small step could Vijay take to extend the pretend play?
qa.a: Keep playing along and let her lead, maybe asking what else the "phone" can do.

qa.q: What is it like for Vijay to be pulled into the game?
qa.a: He seems amused and happy to play along, adding jokes of his own.

grounding: Shows a young child using a banana as a pretend phone with her father joining in.

passage:
Nursery note from Sachin, Monday
Nikita (4) held a birthday party for the teddies today. She stood a wooden block on its end on a plate and said, "Cake." Then she pushed three pencils into the playdough on top: "Candles." She blew them out and cut the block with a paper knife. When another child took a "slice", she said, "Say thank you!" I joined in and sang. Tomorrow I'll add some old boxes to the pretend corner.

qa.q: What did Nikita use as a cake?
qa.a: A wooden block stood on its end.

qa.q: What does Nikita saying "Say thank you!" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She was fully caught up in the pretend party and felt proud of hosting it.

qa.q: Why is adding old boxes a good idea for the pretend corner?
qa.a: Open-ended objects let children decide what they stand for, which feeds this kind of play.

qa.q: How might the child who took a "slice" feel?
qa.a: Included and happy to be part of Nikita's pretend party.

grounding: Shows a young child using blocks and pencils to stand for a cake and candles in pretend play.

passage: In their village, Hrithik, five, had a stick he called Badal, his horse. He galloped it round the neem tree every evening. His older sister Seema laughed. "That's just a stick." Hrithik stopped, face red, and hugged the stick to his chest. "It's Badal!" Seema saw his face and changed her tone. "Sorry. Does Badal want water?" She put a leaf in front of it. Hrithik brightened and made Badal drink.

qa.q: What did Hrithik call his stick?
qa.a: He called it Badal, his horse.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik's face go red when Seema laughed?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry that she mocked Badal, who was real to him in the game.

qa.q: What did Seema do to repair things?
qa.a: She said sorry and joined the pretend game by offering the horse water, which respected his idea.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had kept laughing?
qa.a: Hrithik might have stopped playing or stayed resentful towards her.

grounding: Shows a young child using a stick as a horse in pretend play and his hurt when an older sister dismisses it.

passage: In a park in Copenhagen, Lars, five, found a forked stick. "This is my magic wand," he told Paulo. He waved it at a pigeon. "Now you're a dragon!" Paulo picked up a flat stone. "This is my phone. I'm calling the dragon police." He held it to his ear. "Hello? Send a big net." Lars used a leaf as the net and swooped it over the pigeon, which flew away. "It escaped!" they both shouted, delighted.

qa.q: What did Paulo use as a phone?
qa.a: A flat stone.

qa.q: How did Lars feel when the pigeon flew away?
qa.a: Lars felt delighted and excited, shouting with Paulo.

qa.q: How could a parent support this kind of pretend play?
qa.a: Offer open-ended objects like sticks and stones, join the story briefly, and let the children lead.

qa.q: How might Paulo see Lars's wand idea?
qa.a: Paulo seems to enjoy it and joins in, adding his own pretend phone to the story.

grounding: In a Danish park, two five-year-olds turn sticks, stones and leaves into a wand, a phone and a net.

passage: In December the kindergarten's dress-up box was full of leftovers from the Christmas play. Imran, five, picked up a cardboard tube. "Telescope!" He peered at the ceiling. "I see a ship!" Then he turned it sideways. "Now it's a trumpet." Tooot. Ayesha Ma'am handed him a paper plate. Imran held it like a steering wheel. "Now I'm driving to the moon!" A friend tried to take the tube; Imran scowled, then handed it over and made a new trumpet from his fist.

qa.q: What did Imran first call the cardboard tube?
qa.a: A telescope.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he scowled at his friend?
qa.a: Imran felt annoyed and a little resentful at having his tube taken.

qa.q: How did Ayesha Ma'am encourage Imran's pretend play?
qa.a: She handed him another open-ended object, a paper plate, which he turned into a steering wheel.

qa.q: How might the friend feel receiving the tube?
qa.a: The friend was probably pleased and excited to play with it.

grounding: In a December kindergarten, a five-year-old turns a tube and a plate into many pretend objects.

passage: I'm Kashish, Ankita's older sister. In wedding season, after we came home from our cousin's sangeet, Ankita, five, wouldn't stop playing wedding. She draped Mummy's dupatta over her head and said it was a veil. A steel ladle became her microphone. "Now the band!" She made me bang a pot. Then she tied a red ribbon on our teddy and said he was the groom. I don't know how she thinks of all this. She even pretended scraps of paper were petals and threw them at the teddy.

qa.q: What did Ankita use as a microphone?
qa.a: A steel ladle.

qa.q: What might Ankita have been feeling during the pretend wedding?
qa.a: Ankita seemed excited and happy, full of ideas after the sangeet.

qa.q: How could Kashish join in to support Ankita's pretend play?
qa.a: Kashish could take a role, like the band or a guest, and follow Ankita's story without taking over.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Ankita's imagination?
qa.a: Kashish is amused and a little amazed, not knowing how Ankita thinks of all these uses.

grounding: An older sister describes a five-year-old using household objects to stage a pretend wedding in wedding season.

passage:
First day of Ganesh festival: Damini holds a banana to her ear. "Hello, Ganpati Bappa?" Manoj laughs.

Three days later: she puts a shoebox on the table, drapes a dupatta on it, and says, "This is the mandap." She sits her doll inside.

Last day of the festival: she waves a stick with a marigold on top. "This is my aarti," she sings, walking round the shoebox.

qa.q: What did Damini put her doll inside?
qa.a: She sat her doll inside the shoebox mandap.

qa.q: How was Damini feeling when she waved the marigold stick?
qa.a: Damini was happy and absorbed in her pretend festival, singing as she walked around.

qa.q: How can Manoj encourage Damini's pretend play?
qa.a: He can join in, pretend with her, and give her more everyday things like boxes and cloth.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel watching Damini's play grow?
qa.a: Manoj was amused at first and likely delighted to see her imagination grow.

grounding: Over the Ganesh festival days, a child uses everyday objects to represent a phone, a mandap and an aarti lamp.

passage:
The train to Pune was hot and noisy in the summer holidays, and the fan in their coach wasn't working. Ritu and Kashish, both five, were restless.

Ritu grabbed a steel spoon. "This is a mic! I'm a singer!"

Kashish tied a towel around her neck. "I'm a superhero!"

They put on a show in the aisle. Other passengers clapped, and even the tired ticket checker smiled.

qa.q: What did Ritu use as a mic?
qa.a: She grabbed a steel spoon.

qa.q: How did Ritu and Kashish feel putting on their show?
qa.a: They were excited and happy, performing for the passengers.

qa.q: How can adults encourage children's pretend play on long journeys?
qa.a: Offer safe everyday objects like spoons and towels and let them invent their own games.

qa.q: How might the ticket checker feel seeing the show?
qa.a: The ticket checker was tired but amused, smiling at their play.

grounding: On a hot, noisy train journey in the summer holidays, children use a spoon as a mic and a towel as a cape in pretend play.

passage:
During Christmas week in Bengaluru, Yusuf, five, grabbed the broom and galloped around the flat. "My horse is going to Bethlehem!"

His sister Nandini put a paper crown on. "I'm a king. Wait for me!"

Yusuf reined in his broom. "My horse is tired. It needs water." He made slurping sounds.

Nandini laughed and handed him a cup. "For your horse."

qa.q: What did Yusuf use as a horse?
qa.a: He grabbed the broom.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel galloping with the broom?
qa.a: Yusuf was excited and joyful, deep in his pretend journey.

qa.q: How did Nandini support Yusuf's pretend play?
qa.a: She joined his story as a king and gave his horse water, building on his idea.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel joining the game?
qa.a: Nandini seemed amused and happy to play along.

grounding: During Christmas week, a child turns a broom into a horse, and his sister joins his pretend story.

passage:
"This is my magic wand," said Tanuja, waving a twig she'd found outside the Durga Puja pandal.
"It's just a stick," said her sister Shalini.
"No! It turns you into a frog. Zap!"
Shalini crossed her arms. "I wanted that stick for my flag."
"Frogs can't have flags. Ribbit!"
"Maa, she always takes the best things!"
Maa looked up. "Tanuja, can the wand make flags too?"
Tanuja thought. "Zap! Now it's your flag, Shalini. You're not a frog anymore."
Shalini sniffed, then grinned and waved it.

qa.q: What did Tanuja say her wand does?
qa.a: It turns you into a frog.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she crossed her arms?
qa.a: She felt resentful and left out, because she had wanted the stick for her flag.

qa.q: How did Maa's question help the sisters?
qa.a: It invited Tanuja to use her pretend idea to share, so the stick could be a wand and a flag without a fight. 👍

qa.q: What would change if Maa had just taken the stick away?
qa.a: The pretend game would stop, and both girls might end up feeling cross instead of playing together.

grounding: Illustrates a young child turning a twig into a pretend wand, and then into a flag to share with her sister.
